questions.stem: Sam, 73, is sitting bolt upright on an ED trolley. His RR is 34 and SpO2 86% on room air, and he says, "Don't lie me down, I can't breathe flat." You now want to examine his neck veins. How should you assess his jugular venous pressure?
options: Lie him flat briefly so the neck veins fill, then measure from the sternal angle
Assess him sitting upright; a venous pulsation above the clavicle means a raised JVP
Skip the JVP and use ankle oedema as the marker of right-sided filling pressure
Recline him to 45° for a minute, because the JVP is only reliably measured at that angle
questions.why: The sternal angle stays about 5 cm above the right atrium in any position, so you can assess the JVP with him sitting at 90°. If a venous pulsation is visible above the clavicle while he is fully upright, his JVP is clearly raised. Never lie an orthopnoeic patient flat.
notes: Lying him flat will make his orthopnoea and hypoxaemia worse. Also, the neck veins fill when lying flat even when the JVP is normal, so the finding tells you little.
Ankle oedema is a late and insensitive sign, and Sam has not noticed any swelling. Skipping the JVP misses a key sign of congestion.
45° is only a convenient angle and is not needed for a valid reading. Reclining a patient in respiratory distress adds risk and gains nothing.

questions.stem: Sam, 73, has hypertensive acute pulmonary oedema a month after an anterior MI. On oxygen his SpO2 is 92%, but he is still very breathless, with BP 212/112 and HR 114. He takes no PDE5 inhibitor, and CPAP is being set up. Which drug treatment should you start now?
options: IV morphine 2.5 mg, repeated every 5 min, to reduce preload and relieve his air hunger
IV metoprolol 5 mg, repeated, to slow the tachycardia and lower his BP
Sublingual GTN 400 microgram spray every 5 min while systolic BP stays above 100 mmHg
Oral amlodipine 10 mg to bring his blood pressure down over the next few hours
questions.why: Nitrates dilate veins, which lowers preload, and at higher doses dilate arteries, which lowers afterload. This gives rapid relief in hypertensive APO. Repeat sublingual GTN, then start an IV infusion titrated to response, and hold it if systolic BP falls below 100 mmHg or if a PDE5 inhibitor has been taken.
notes: Morphine is no longer routinely recommended in APO. It causes respiratory depression and vomiting and is linked to worse outcomes, including more need for ventilation.
His sinus tachycardia is compensating for a failing ventricle. Giving an IV beta-blocker during acute decompensation can tip him into cardiogenic shock.
Oral amlodipine acts slowly and does not reduce preload. It has no role in the emergency management of acute pulmonary oedema.

questions.stem: Sam, 73, on perindopril after an anterior MI, took regular ibuprofen for 2 weeks for back pain. His creatinine rose from 95 to 150 µmol/L and he developed acute pulmonary oedema. Which mechanism best explains how the ibuprofen contributed?
options: Blocking renal prostaglandins, constricting afferent arterioles and retaining Na+
Blocking cardiac L-type calcium channels, reducing contractility over several days
Blocking angiotensin II action at the efferent arteriole, lowering glomerular pressure
Activating PPAR-gamma in the collecting duct, increasing sodium reabsorption
questions.why: Prostaglandins keep the afferent arteriole dilated and promote sodium excretion when the kidney is underperfused. NSAIDs block them, so GFR falls (worse with an ACE inhibitor, which dilates the efferent arteriole) and the body retains salt and water. That fluid load overwhelmed his failing ventricle.
notes: Negative inotropy through calcium channel blockade is how verapamil and diltiazem worsen heart failure, not how NSAIDs do.
Loss of angiotensin II tone at the efferent arteriole is the effect of his perindopril, not of ibuprofen.
PPAR-gamma activation causing fluid retention is the mechanism of glitazones such as pioglitazone.

questions.stem: Sam, 73, had an MI treated with a coronary stent a month ago and now has heart failure. Today's ECG is unchanged from his discharge ECG. It shows Q waves in V1 to V3, poor R wave progression and T wave inversion in V1 to V4. Occlusion of which artery most likely caused this infarct?
options: Right coronary artery, occluded in its proximal segment
Left circumflex artery, occluded at its proximal segment
Posterior descending artery, occluded near its origin
questions.why: Leads V1 to V4 look at the septum and anterior wall, which the left anterior descending artery supplies. An anterior infarct damages a large area of left ventricular muscle, so it commonly leads to reduced ejection fraction and heart failure.
notes: The right coronary artery usually supplies the inferior wall, so its infarcts show changes in II, III and aVF, not the anterior chest leads.
The circumflex supplies the lateral wall, so its infarcts show changes in I, aVL, V5 and V6, or posterior changes. They do not cause anterior Q waves.
The posterior descending artery supplies the inferior wall and the posterior part of the septum. Its occlusion causes inferior or posterior changes, not Q waves in V1 to V3.
